title: The Old Woman's Blessing
summary: Akbar rescues an old woman's cow from a ditch and receives a blessing that puzzles his courtiers. Birbal explains the beauty of the old woman's words.
full_text:
While riding in disguise through a village near Fatehpur Sikri, Emperor Akbar and Birbal encountered an elderly, frail widow weeping beside a muddy roadside ditch. Her only cow had slipped into the deep mire and was unable to climb out.

Without hesitation, Emperor Akbar dismounted, rolled up his sleeves, waded into the mud, and helped the old woman push the heavy cow back onto dry land.

Wiping the mud from her cow's flank, the grateful old woman looked at the strong, disguised stranger and blessed him with heartfelt emotion:

'May you become a royal clerk in the court of Emperor Akbar, my son! May you earn five silver rupees every month and never know hunger!'

Akbar smiled, thanked her, and rode away. Back at the palace, Akbar recounted the story to his courtiers, laughing: 'Imagine! I am the Emperor of all Hindustan, master of three hundred kingdoms and millions of gold mohurs, yet she blessed me to become a humble clerk earning five silver rupees a month!'

The courtiers mocked the old woman's ignorance, but Birbal remained thoughtful.

'Birbal,' Akbar asked, 'do you also find her blessing amusing?'

Birbal replied with gentle warmth: 'Sire, her blessing was the highest praise she could conceive. In her small world, a royal clerk in your court is the most exalted, secure, and respected person she knows, and five silver rupees is a king's fortune that would feed her family for a year.

'She did not give you a meager wish; she wished upon you the very summit of security and honor within her imagination! A blessing is measured not by the words spoken, but by the fullness of love and gratitude in the heart of the one who gives it.'

Akbar was deeply touched by Birbal's insight. He ordered a comfortable cottage, five dairy cows, and a monthly pension of ten silver rupees sent to the old woman, proving that an Emperor's true glory lies in understanding the humble hearts of his people.
moral: A sincere blessing from the grateful poor is worth more than all the crowns of kings.
